Key Takeaways
  • Decoys should look and behave like the environment around them, not just appear convincing on a dashboard.
  • Placement matters more than decoy count. Deception is most useful when attackers encounter it along realistic attack paths.
  • A high-confidence alert is only the starting point. The real value comes from knowing which endpoint or identity triggered it, what happened beforehand, and where the attacker tried to move next.
  • Identity deception deserves as much attention as network deception.
  • “Agentless” should not be treated as a checkbox. Buyers should look at what actually needs to be deployed, what touches production systems, how much maintenance is required, and whether the architecture works across cloud, OT, legacy, and unmanaged environments.
  • Deception has to keep changing with the environment. Static decoys become easier to spot and harder to manage. Automated discovery and lifecycle management help keep the deception believable as infrastructure changes.
  • Fidelis brings the pieces together rather than treating deception as an isolated trap.

A cyber deception solution is easy to describe in a demo. Deploy a few decoys, scatter deceptive credentials around the environment, wait for an attacker to touch one, and generate an alert.

Evaluating whether that deception will actually work across a large enterprise is considerably harder.

The bigger question is: Will an attacker encounter the deception, believe it, and generate enough evidence for the SOC to act?

Deception is no longer simply a honeypot at a larger scale. Modern deception can span endpoints, networks, identities, Active Directory, cloud infrastructure, OT environments, credentials, data, applications, and likely attack paths.

The UK National Cyber Security Centre[1] has been testing that operational reality. Its cyber deception initiative involved 121 organizations, 14 commercial providers, and 10 product trials across environments ranging from cloud to operational technology. The NCSC found genuine potential for detecting novel threats and enriching threat intelligence, but also emphasized that deception is not plug-and-play. Its effectiveness depends on context, configuration, maintenance, and a clear strategy.

For security leaders conducting a deception technology comparison, that is an important distinction. The decision should not come down to the number of decoys in a licensing tier or the longest feature list. It should come down to whether the platform can make deception believable, put it where attackers are likely to encounter it, keep it current, and turn an interaction into something the SOC can investigate.

Here are 12 capabilities worth testing.

1. Deception That Remains Convincing Under Inspection

Start with realism.

A decoy may look perfectly legitimate on a product dashboard but fail the moment an attacker begins interrogating it.

Reconnaissance can expose operating systems, open ports, service banners, applications, DNS information, naming conventions, directory relationships, files, and other characteristics. A fake SQL server that behaves nothing like the production SQL servers around it is not much of a trap.

MITRE’s adversary-engagement[2] guidance points to the same problem. Traditional honeypots can be unrealistic, easily signatured, and overly generic. MITRE instead advocates engagement environments tailored to their surroundings and instrumented around the defender’s objective.

Ask the vendor to demonstrate what happens when the decoy is interrogated more deeply.

A mature deception solution should support the appropriate mix of emulated and higher-interaction systems. Lightweight emulation is useful when scale matters. More interactive environments may make sense when the objective is to observe attacker behavior in greater detail. The requirement is the right fidelity for the risk and use case.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception® builds decoys using context from the real environment. Its decoys can reproduce real operating systems and services, open ports, applications, files, folders, and other characteristics that an attacker would expect to see. Its deception architecture can include both actual and emulated operating systems and applications rather than forcing one interaction model everywhere.

More importantly, Fidelis does not treat realism as a one-time configuration exercise. Its decoys can be automatically updated to mirror changes in the surrounding environment.

For a buyer, that matters more than how convincing a decoy looks on deployment day.

2. High-Confidence Alerts with Enough Context to Investigate

Deception has an inherent detection advantage: legitimate users and applications generally have little reason to interact with something deliberately created to be fake.

A production administrator launching PowerShell may be legitimate. An unusual authentication could have an innocent explanation. An endpoint attempting to authenticate to a deceptive server using a credential that no legitimate user should possess is a different kind of signal.

But there is an important distinction: High confidence does not automatically mean high context.

An alert saying “Host 10.20.30.15 interacted with decoy server” gives the SOC a strong starting point, but the analyst still needs answers:

  • Which endpoint initiated the interaction?
  • Which identity or credential was involved?
  • What did the system do before reaching the decoy?
  • Was there reconnaissance or lateral movement?
  • What happened next?

Good deception technology features should shorten the distance between the trigger and those answers.

How Fidelis addresses this

Fidelis Deception generates alerts when attackers interact with decoys, fake credentials, deceptive data, fake accounts, or other deliberately planted assets.

Fidelis deception events can be enriched with network, endpoint, sandbox, and threat context, allowing an analyst to move beyond the isolated decoy event and investigate the activity around it.

That is the capability buyers should test: not simply whether the deception alert is accurate, but how much investigation remains after it fires.

3. Automated Discovery Before Decoy Deployment

Good deception starts by understanding what is real.

Before deciding what to fake, the platform should understand relevant assets, operating systems, services, applications, identities, communication relationships, and exposures.

Otherwise, teams risk creating technically functional decoys that do not fit their surroundings. The challenge becomes more obvious six months after deployment.

Servers have been added. Applications have moved. New cloud resources exist. Active Directory has changed. Older workloads have disappeared.

If the deception layer still represents the environment as it looked during implementation, credibility gradually erodes.

A dashboard showing 5,000 deployed decoys looks impressive. It does not necessarily mean an attacker will encounter one.

Attackers do not move evenly across an enterprise. They follow credentials, trust relationships, shared services, administrative paths, cloud permissions, accessible systems, and opportunities to gain privilege.

Deception should therefore intersect likely attacker movement, not simply mirror the CMDB.

Consider a domain controller.

Protecting it does not necessarily mean placing another fake domain controller next to it. The stronger approach may be planting credentials, mapped drives, accounts, shares, or breadcrumbs at the points an attacker would investigate before reaching the real domain controller.

Fidelis Deception maps relationships between users, systems, and data to provide visibility into potential attack paths and movement patterns. Fidelis then uses that context to place deception where attackers are more likely to operate.

Its approach also uses breadcrumbs to intentionally pull an attacker from something real toward something deceptive. That makes the meaningful metric less about decoy density and more about attacker encounter probability.

A deception strategy focused only on network assets leaves a major part of the attack surface untouched.

MITRE ATT&CK documents[3] the use of valid accounts across domain, local, cloud, and other account types. Once an adversary has legitimate credentials, authentication activity can become considerably harder to separate from normal behavior.

Deceptive identities change that equation.

  • honey credentials,
  • fake service accounts,
  • deceptive AD users and computer objects,
  • tokens and keys,
  • cached credentials,
  • misleading directory relationships,
  • and other identity artifacts appropriate to the environment.

If an adversary retrieves and uses a credential that should never have been used by anyone, intent becomes much clearer.

Fidelis has extended deception specifically into Active Directory through Fidelis Active Directory Intercept.

Attackers do not respect product boundaries.

An intrusion can begin on an endpoint, discover credentials, query Active Directory, move across the network, authenticate to a cloud workload, and eventually approach OT or IoT systems. Deception should be able to follow that path.

A modern deception solution should not reduce the category to fake servers. Different attack stages create different opportunities to deceive.

Too many descriptions of deception end here: Attacker touches decoy → Alert fires.

Deployment architecture deserves careful scrutiny. But buyers should avoid reducing the decision to agentless deception being good and agent deception as bad. Real architectures are more nuanced.

A platform may avoid installing software on production endpoints while still using sensors, virtual appliances, containers, integrations, or centralized deception infrastructure. items.title: How “123456” became the key to almost 9 million personal records
items.summary: An attacker reportedly used a leaked password to abuse a company’s legitimate access to Denmark’s population register (CPR). The weak password is remarkable, but the failure to spot millions of unusual searches made the breach worse. The CPR administration states it identified a serious security incident. By abusing a Danish company’s authorized access to the CPR system, unauthorized people gained access to the names, addresses, CPR numbers, and other information belonging to around 8.8 million people registered in the system. CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. How could a password so weak that it should have been rejected by the system open the door to so much personal information ? The attacker reportedly gained access through Pays ApS, an IT company based in Odense. According to TV 2 , Pays has confirmed that its authorized access to search the CPR system was abused. Pays offers services including data updates and “CPR cleansing,” allowing customers to check records against the register to update addresses, identify people who have died, and obtain information about changes of address. The attacker reportedly used a leaked password associated with a former Pays employee. TV 2 says an email containing the password 123456 had appeared in a larger data leak, and that this account of the initial access matches its own research. The attackers had access for 21 days before it was shut down on October 2, although the suspicious activity appears to have stopped on September 20. An unusually large bill for around 14 million searches drew attention to the breach. Politiken reports that the data stolen in those searches belonged to approximately 5.5 million living and 3.3 million deceased people. A weak, leaked password opened an authorized route into a sensitive register. That access allowed millions of searches, and the activity was discovered only after an unusually large bill drew attention to it. How to stay safe If your organization handles sensitive data: Don’t reuse passwords or use personal passwords for work accounts. Use a password manager to create and remember strong, unique passwords for you. For systems that give access to sensitive data, enforce authentication that would reject weak passwords and make multi-factor authentication mandatory. Monitor for unusual activity. That many searches from one account should have been noticed earlier. If your data may have been exposed in this breach: Keep an eye on official updates about the incident. items.title: IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs
items.summary: IBM patched 22 vulnerabilities in Verify Identity Access and Security Verify Access, including two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated remote code execution across appliance and container deployments. The most severe bugs, CVE-2026-78401 and CVE-2026-78406, each carry a CVSS score of 9.8. Both involve deserializing untrusted data, a process where software rebuilds stored or transmitted data into objects without properly checking whether it is safe. The publicly listed advisory for CVE-2026-78401 confirms the risk of unauthenticated remote code execution . IBM rates both deserialization bugs as network-accessible attacks with low complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction.IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs. items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Webshells and XMRig Miners
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting two flaws in AhsayCBS backup servers to run commands, plant webshells, and install XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised as Microsoft Edge. Huntress first observed exploitation on October 7, 2026, at 23:20:15 UTC. By October 8, its researchers had seen five organizations targeted, with attackers checking systems and setting up tools to maintain access. The campaign targets Ahsay Cloud Backup Server, a management platform used by managed service providers and system integrators. Administrators use it to manage backup users, policies, and operations. According to Huntress’s investigation , versions up to 10.3.4 are affected, including a release previously described as safe. The attack chains CVE-2026-105133, a medium-severity authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function, with CVE-2026-105134, a critical flaw in the Replication Receiver endpoint at /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Together, they let attackers bypass login checks and execute commands as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, giving them broad control over the Windows host. Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws The NVD entry for CVE-2026-105134, published October 4, lists a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and describes remote command injection. It still identifies version 10.3.4 as a fix. However, Huntress’s October 8 update says that the version remains vulnerable, making the conflicting guidance important for administrators assessing exposure. VirusTotal results for msedge.exe (source: Huntress ) After gaining access, attackers configured a malicious replication receiver and placed Java Server Page webshells inside the application’s web directory. Huntress also detected suspicious commands launched by cbssvcX64.exe, the AhsayCBS service executable. This pattern resembles earlier z0Miner attacks against WebLogic servers , where attackers used JSP webshells to maintain access before deploying mining tools. That similarity describes a shared method, not evidence that the campaigns involve the same operators. Attackers downloaded Taskgmr.ps1, edge.exe, msedge.exe, and config.json into temporary folders from an Alibaba Cloud Object Storage endpoint. The file edge.exe was XMRig, while msedge.exe was a modified copy of NSSM, a legitimate utility that keeps other programs running. A newly created Windows service, MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc, ran the disguised NSSM binary with SYSTEM privileges. It kept the miner active and restarted it after crashes or reboots. The miner connected to xmr. kryptex[.]network and 51.195.127[.]124 on port 8029. The use of webshells followed by Monero mining also appears in earlier Apache web server coinminer attacks , highlighting how exposed servers can become income sources for attackers. The PowerShell script monitored Task Manager and stopped the mining service whenever users opened it. Mining resumed after Task Manager was closed. items.title: FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Executive in ShinyHunters-Linked Extortion Investigation
items.summary: The FBI arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky in Pennsylvania on October 8, 2026, as part of its investigation into the hacking group ShinyHunters . The arrest links a professional involved in ransomware response to an alleged cyber extortion conspiracy. However, the evidence behind the charges remains largely sealed, and the allegations have not been proven in court. According to KrebsOnSecurity, Dubrovsky was associated with Canadian security firm CyberSteward and had planned to attend a cyber insurance conference in Philadelphia. Sources told the publication that the arrested Canadian was visiting Pennsylvania for the event. The Cyber Risk Summit ran from October 5 through October 7 at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel. The public court docket lists the defendant as Edward Dobrovsky, a slightly different spelling. FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Executive in ShinyHunters KrebsOnSecurity reported charges involving conspiracy to threaten the confidentiality of information to extort money and interference with commerce through threats. With the main complaint sealed, the public record does not explain what actions prosecutors allege Dobrovsky took. An October 9 court order committed the defendant to the Eastern District of Texas. Records also show that a judge appointed federal defenders and ordered detention pending a hearing in the charging district. This updates an important detail in the initial reporting, which said Dubrovsky had not yet received appointed counsel. Cypfer, another Canadian cybersecurity company, disputed Dubrovsky’s claim that he was a former founder. In an October 10 update, a company spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity that he had served as managing director, not founder or co-founder, and resigned in November 2025. The distinction prevents his arrest from being wrongly presented as the arrest of Cypfer’s founder. Indexed at Courtlistener (source : krebsonsecurity ) ShinyHunters typically steals login details through phishing and uses compromised accounts to take data from cloud software services. The group then threatens to publish stolen records unless victims pay. KrebsOnSecurity, citing the FBI, reported that the group had extorted more than $70 million from victims during 2026. The investigation also covers the theft of sensitive information from the FBI’s recruitment portal. The New York Times reported that stolen records included home addresses, Social Security numbers , and sensitive job assignments. KrebsOnSecurity said the exposed material included medical and psychiatric information. Such records create concerns beyond financial loss because they reveal deeply personal details about bureau personnel. The case follows the arrest of an alleged ShinyHunters leader in the Netherlands . Dutch police detained a 24-year-old Amsterdam suspect on September 15 with FBI support. A security company executive identified him as Pepijn van der Stap, although Dutch authorities did not publicly name him. His alleged role remains unproven. Another development involved Saif al-Din Khader, reportedly known online as Rey. Cybersecurity News previously reported that the suspected ShinyHunters member helped FBI investigators after detention in Jordan. That reported cooperation does not establish his role in the FBI breach or validate every claim made by the hacking group. For readers following the case, the key gap remains Dubrovsky’s alleged conduct. Public reporting establishes an arrest and allegations of extortion, but the sealed complaint limits scrutiny of the evidence. Further court filings may clarify how prosecutors connect his work to ShinyHunters. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. Integrate ANYRUN’s Sandbox in your SOC

items.title: DTX + UCX 2026: Ingram Micro on Unlocking AI and Cloud Without Losing Control
items.summary: Ahead of their participation at DTX + UCX London 2026 , Lee Robson, AWS Greenfield Practice Lead at Ingram Micro shares what the company will be showcasing at the event and explains what trends will impact the channel in the year ahead. How is Ingram Micro participating in DTX + UCX 2026? Ingram Micro will be showcasing how organisations can accelerate innovation with AWS. Our team will be demonstrating practical AI, cloud and security solutions, including AWS Quick , Claude via Amazon Bedrock , FinOps-led cloud optimisation and AWS security assessments . We’ll be connecting customers with specialist partners that can help turn strategy into measurable business outcomes. What are the key messages you will be promoting to delegates of the show? Our message is simple: unlock the value of AI and cloud while maintaining control of cost, security and governance. We’ll be highlighting how AWS enables organisations to innovate faster, connect apps, data, and teams so answers turn into action instantly with AWS Quick, adopt generative AI through Claude via Bedrock, optimise cloud spend through FinOps, and strengthen their security posture. What are the biggest challenges organisations face when purchasing technology through the channel? Many organisations are overwhelmed by the pace of technology change, particularly around AI and cloud. Common challenges include understanding where to start, selecting the right solutions, managing cloud costs, ensuring security and compliance, and finding the skills required to implement and support new technologies successfully. How can dedicated, experienced partners solve these challenges? Experienced partners help customers move from technology discussions to business outcomes. With Ingram Micro, they remove the barrier to entry for a lot of businesses and provide strategic guidance, technical expertise and proven delivery frameworks that reduce risk and accelerate adoption. Partners can also help organisations optimise AWS investments, implement AI responsibly, improve security and create clear roadmaps for long-term success. What trends do you believe will impact the channel in the year ahead? Generative AI adoption will continue to accelerate, but organisations will increasingly focus on governance, security and achieving measurable ROI. We also expect greater emphasis on FinOps as cloud estates mature, alongside growing demand for cybersecurity services. Partners that combine AI expertise, cloud optimisation and security capabilities will be best positioned for growth.

items.title: Pluralistic: How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist (12 Oct 2026)
items.summary: Today's links How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist : If you care about labor justice and artists' rights, stop focusing on copyright. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : China unblocks Wikipedia; CCC cracks the Bundestrojaner; "Children of the Sky"; "Messy"; Every top Icelandic banker is guilty; Climate activism x digital activism; Gene Kan on P2P's future; Larry Ellison x mass surveillance; W3C v patents; "Work from home" in the cybercrime supply-chain; "Nursery Rhyme Comics"; Glitchy tea-set; Tourist Guy; Vista v reinstallation; Ryanair v your bladder; Wells Fargo CEO loves "sales culture"; "Attention Merchants"; Orban v free press; AI v GIGO; Dylan wins the Nobel; India's starving kids app; Adobe's spyware copyfraud; Charter blackmails customers with bad credit threats; Fix UK housing. Upcoming appearances : Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Kilkenny, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. How labor rights rescued Ultima from a monopolist ( permalink ) If you work in the media, you have doubtless had a lifetime of encouragement to treat copyright as your primary source of economic protection, and doubtless you've been told that this protection arises from the fact that copyright is a property right – specifically, it's a subspecies of "intellectual property": https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-ip/ Property rights are capitalism's holy sacrament, so of course, it's natural to treasure any property right you can lay claim to. But this is a trap. Creative workers aren't asset speculators , we're workers . When we bargain with a media company to sell them our copyright, we're just bargaining to sell our labor , not our property . This is a distinction with a difference. Property rights are alienable . When you negotiate to sell your property to someone else, you propose to transfer the title to that property. If you sell your house, you don't get to move back in if you change your mind later. Sell your car, and you must not get in and drive it away. Nominally, creative workers only bargain away some of their copyright, because copyright is also divisible . You can sell US English print rights to a novel, a one-month license to synch a song to an advertisement, or the right to display a painting for a year. But here's the thing about property rights: the most reliable predictor of how many property rights you must give up in a sale isn't how many property rights you started with – it's how much bargaining power you have. For 50 years, governments have expanded copyright in every way, making it last longer, cover more works and restrict more uses, all backstopped by ever-steepening penalties. 50 years later, media companies – our bosses – are larger and more profitable than they've ever been, and we're poorer than we've ever been. The share of the money generated by our labor has declined, even as our rights over the product of that labor have expanded. How to make sense of this? It's easy, once you factor in power . In a world of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies and a single ebook/audiobook company, getting more copyright to bargain with just means getting more copyright to bargain away . When copyright's term expanded from "life plus 50 years" to "life plus 70 years," our bosses simply demanded the entirety of the new term, and didn't offer us a dime more. This is the thesis of Chokepoint Capitalism , the book on Big Tech, Big Media, and creative labor markets Rebecca Giblin and I published in 2022: https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx Chokepoint Capitalism is broken into two parts: the first half of the book is a series of pitiless, plain-language dissections of the baroque scams that media companies have used to make themselves richer from our work, from Spotify to Amazon to Livenation and beyond. From reader feedback, I can tell you that these chapters will make you very angry, because once you strip away all the deliberate obfuscation, all you're left with is one screw-job after another, each of which makes the creators you love poorer even as you pay more for their work. But then there's the second half of the book. This section is devoted to "shovel-ready" policy solutions, each of which is designed to change the "distribution" of the spoils of the media industry, putting more money in workers' pockets at the expense of our bosses. None of these are things you can do as a "conscious consumer." The monopolistic destruction of creators' livelihoods is a systemic problem and you can't solve it by shopping better. The point of these chapters is to lay out what we must demand from our policymakers when (inevitably), they propose to "solve" the problem of worsening straits for creative workers – and to help creative workers understand that when our bosses demand more copyright, that's not there to benefit us . One of these systemic solutions is "termination of transfer," a simple and radical idea that has a proven track-record of making creative workers richer at our bosses' expense. Simply put, "termination of transfer" is the statutory right to void any contract you've signed to transfer your copyright to someone else. In the USA, the 1976 Copyright Act introduced a 35-year termination right. 35 years after you sign any copyright contract, you can file some paperwork with the US Copyright Office and get that copyright back, no matter what your contract says . From The Babysitters Club to the early Stephen King novels to George Clinton's entire catalog, termination of transfer has put lots of money into creative workers' pockets at the expense of corporations that ripped them off at the start of their careers. From the start, there was no question whether termination of transfer would make it into Chokepoint Capitalism . If we want to make creative workers richer, changing the 35-year administrative right into an automatic 20-year termination right is a no-brainer amendment to copyright law. On the Techjess podcast, Garriott marveled at how easy the process was: "there’s a really weird United States copyright law that says if you are the original holder of a copyright and you assign it or sell it to any publisher or any other entity, after 35 years, you can just take it back":

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2El7VtPuSzs

EA killed off Ultima in 2000, and it has languished since, despite an ardent fandom. Garriott has vowed to reissue the old games and is mulling new ones.

All this brings me back to property rights. Property rights are uniquely unsuitable to this kind of arrangement. You don't get to move back into the house your parents sold 35 years ago, and if you did, the photographer who took the family portrait in the hallway wouldn't be allowed to break in and take it away 35 years after you sat for it.

Termination of transfer isn't an "IP right" – it's a labor right. It belongs to the large class of rights that are far more important and useful than mere property rights, such as privacy rights and human rights:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/28/cost-of-everything/#value-of-nothing

If copyright were just about property rights, then termination of transfer would be inconceivable. Termination is a vestigial labor right at the very periphery of copyright. It protects artists, and it can only do so because it is not a property right.

This is one of the themes in The Bezzle, my 2024 historical technothriller, starring my two-fisted forensic accountant hero Martin Hench who uses termination to help an artist claw back his rights from an unscrupulous former manager who forged his signature decades before (this plotline is based on the true story of Parliament/Funkadelic's George Clinton!):

https://craphound.com/bezzle/

If you signed away your rights 35 years ago and want to get them back, check out the Authors Alliance, a nonprofit whose advisory board I volunteer for. We produced a tool that automates all the hardest parts of terminating your transfers and getting your rights back:

https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/

Some of our most ardent fans are academics, whose publicly funded papers are published in journals dominated by a cartel of giant companies that do not pay the authors, nor the editors, nor the reviewers, but still claim all rights and charge the institutions that funded the research they publish tens of thousands of dollars per journal to access that research:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/16/the-public-sphere/#not-the-elsevier

But it's not just academics who have an interest in termination of transfer. It's video game authors, novelists, musicians – and maybe you, someday!

items.title: From zero to agent builder: Running kagent on your laptop
items.summary: If you have seen a demo of a no-code agent builder, you know the moment. Someone types one sentence, waits a minute, and there it is: a new agent, running, with tools. It is impressive. For about ten seconds. Then the questions start. Where does it run? What can it touch? Who approved it? This post is about the first part, the ten impressive seconds. I want to show that it is not magic and that you can build it yourself, in an afternoon, with open source and spending a minimum on tokens. The tool is kagent , a CNCF Sandbox project that runs AI agents as Kubernetes resources. The questions come back at the end, because they are the real work. Why kagent makes this almost boring In kagent, an agent is not a process you start by hand. It is a custom resource. You write an Agent with a system prompt, a model, and a list of tools. You apply it, and the controller turns it into a running pod that speaks A2A . Once agents are just YAML, an agent that builds agents is simply an agent that can write one kind of YAML. No new framework, no plugin. One Agent , three tools, and a prompt that knows what an Agent looks like. Figure 1: An agent that builds agents, on kagent. Before you start: What this lab is not The goal here is the builder. Security is out of scope, on purpose, and I want to be upfront about what that means: kagent runs in its default unsecure auth mode, so every request acts as the same user. The chart’s bundled PostgreSQL uses its built-in password. The UI and API are reachable only through kubectl port-forward on 127.0.0.1. That is fine for a laptop. It is not fine for a shared cluster, and I will come back to why that gap matters. You need Docker, kind, kubectl, helm, jq and Ollama (alternatively, you can use your API Key for Claude, OpenAI, or any other provider, but we wanted to make it as cheap as possible). There is nothing to clone: you create every file as you go. Start in an empty folder: mkdir kagent-agent-builder && cd kagent-agent-builder Step 1: Pick a local model that can actually do it This is the part that surprised me. Writing a valid Kubernetes manifest through a tool call is harder than chatting, and small models show it. In my runs, qwen2.5:7b-instruct invented its own tool block format, and qwen2.5:14b-instruct sometimes answered politely without ever calling the apply tool. qwen3-coder:30b-a3b got it right on every run, so that is the model this post uses: ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M # about 18 GB on disk The cluster reaches Ollama at host.docker.internal:11434, which works out of the box with Docker Desktop. On Linux you have to change that host in the values file below to an address the kind node can reach. I have not tested that path. If you prefer a hosted model, kagent’s Helm chart also has provider blocks for OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI and Gemini. Then it is no longer free, of course. Step 2: Install kagent with a tool server that can only write Agents Create the cluster: kind create cluster --name kagent-builder kagent ships a tool server with Kubernetes tools, and by default the chart gives its ServiceAccount cluster-admin. A builder backed by cluster-admin is a bad idea even on a laptop, so the values file changes that. Create it: providers: default: ollama ollama: provider: Ollama model: "qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M" config: host: host.docker.internal:11434 options: num_ctx: "32768" kagent-tools: tools: enabledTools: - k8s rbac: readOnly: true additionalRules: - apiGroups: ["kagent.dev"] resources: ["agents"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"] grafana-mcp: {enabled: false} k8s-agent: {enabled: false} kgateway-agent: {enabled: false} istio-agent: {enabled: false} promql-agent: {enabled: false} observability-agent: {enabled: false} argo-rollouts-agent: {enabled: false} helm-agent: {enabled: false} cilium-policy-agent: {enabled: false} cilium-manager-agent: {enabled: false} cilium-debug-agent: {enabled: false} The model becomes the default ModelConfig . The tool server loads only its Kubernetes tools (22 of them). And it gets a read-only role plus one extra rule: it may write agents.kagent.dev, nothing else. The last block turns off the sample agents the chart installs by default, so the UI only shows yours. Install the CRDs and kagent 0.10.2 with that file, and wait for the pods: helm upgrade --install kagent-crds oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent-crds \ --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \ --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --create-namespace helm upgrade --install kagent oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent \ --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \ --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --values kagent-values.yaml for d in kagent-controller kagent-ui kagent-tools; do kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent rollout status deploy/$d --timeout=300s done Step 3: The builder is just an agent This is the whole builder. Create the file: apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2 kind: Agent metadata: name: agent-builder namespace: kagent spec: description: Builds new kagent agents from a plain-language description and deploys them. type: Declarative declarative: modelConfig: default-model-config stream: false systemMessage: | You build kagent agents. The user describes, in plain language, an agent they want. You turn that into ONE Kubernetes manifest and apply it. Do not ask follow-up questions: pick sensible defaults and go. How you work, in this order: 1. List the existing agents with k8s_get_resources (resource_type agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent). Pick a name that is not taken; never overwrite an existing agent. 2. Write the manifest in exactly the shape below and apply it with k8s_apply_manifest. The user confirms the apply in the UI; that is expected. 3. Read it back with k8s_get_resource_yaml (resource_type agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent) and look at the Accepted and Ready conditions in its status. Ready can take a few seconds. The manifest must be exactly this shape, and nothing else: apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2 kind: Agent metadata: name: namespace: kagent labels: app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: agent-builder spec: description: |- type: Declarative declarative: modelConfig: default-model-config stream: false systemMessage: | tools: - type: McpServer mcpServer: apiGroup: kagent.dev kind: RemoteMCPServer name: kagent-tool-server toolNames: [ ] Read-only tools you may give it: k8s_get_resources, k8s_get_resource_yaml, k8s_describe_resource, k8s_get_events, k8s_get_pod_logs. Never another kind, never another namespace, never write or delete tools, never more than one document. YAML that does not break: free text always goes in a block scalar, as in the shape above (description with |-, systemMessage with |). In a plain scalar, a colon followed by a space makes the YAML invalid, and a space followed by # silently cuts the value short. When something goes wrong: - If the user rejects the apply, do not retry it and do not read the agent back. Say it was not applied, and stop. - Never create a second resource with another name (-test, -check, -v2) to find out what failed. It tells you nothing and leaves clutter. - Do not name a cause you have not checked. An opaque error is not proof of a name clash, a permission problem or a network issue. - Report the error exactly as the tool returned it, and stop. When it is done, answer in three short lines: the agent's name, what it does, and which tools it can use. Then one more line with its real state from step 3 (Accepted, Ready). Never claim it is ready if it is not. tools: - type: McpServer mcpServer: apiGroup: kagent.dev kind: RemoteMCPServer name: kagent-tool-server toolNames: - k8s_apply_manifest - k8s_get_resources - k8s_get_resource_yaml requireApproval: - k8s_apply_manifest a2aConfig: skills: - id: build-agent name: Build an agent description: Turns a plain-language description into a deployed kagent agent. tags: [builder, agents] examples: - "Create an agent for the support team that answers questions about the state of the services in the cluster" Apply it and wait until kagent reports it Ready: kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder apply -f agent-builder.yaml kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent wait --for=condition=Ready \ agent/agent-builder --timeout=300s The tools block at the end is where the builder gets its limits. toolNames is an allowlist: of the 22 tools on the server, the model sees three. requireApproval is kagent’s human-in-the-loop switch. When the agent calls a tool on that list, the run pauses and the user has to approve or reject the call. The system prompt does the rest. It tells the model to list existing agents first, so it never overwrites one, and then gives it the exact manifest shape it may produce: one Agent , in the kagent namespace, with a label that marks it as built by the builder, and only read-only tools. It also carries a few lessons I learned the hard way. Free text goes in YAML block scalars, because a colon followed by a space inside a plain string breaks the manifest. And when something fails, the model must report the error and stop, not create my-agent-v2 to see what happens. Keep in mind that the prompt is a request, not a guarantee. The guarantees are the allowlist, the approval and RBAC. Step 4: Ask for an agent Open the UI: kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent port-forward \ --address 127.0.0.1 svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080 Go to http://localhost:8080 , pick agent-builder and ask for something: Create an agent for the support team that answers questions about the state of the services in the cluster After half a minute or so the run stops. The UI shows the manifest the model wants to apply and two buttons. Figure 2: The UI showing the manifest requiring user approval before applying. Read it before you click. This is the one moment where a human sees exactly what is about to land in the cluster. items.summary_html:
If you have seen a demo of a no-code agent builder, you know the moment. Someone types one sentence, waits a minute, and there it is: a new agent, running, with tools. It is impressive. For about ten seconds.

Then the questions start. Where does it run? What can it touch? Who approved it?

This post is about the first part, the ten impressive seconds. I want to show that it is not magic and that you can build it yourself, in an afternoon, with open source and spending a minimum on tokens. The tool is kagent, a CNCF Sandbox project that runs AI agents as Kubernetes resources. The questions come back at the end, because they are the real work.

Why kagent makes this almost boring

In kagent, an agent is not a process you start by hand. It is a custom resource. You write an Agent with a system prompt, a model, and a list of tools. You apply it, and the controller turns it into a running pod that speaks A2A.

Once agents are just YAML, an agent that builds agents is simply an agent that can write one kind of YAML. No new framework, no plugin. One Agent, three tools, and a prompt that knows what an Agent looks like.

Figure 1: An agent that builds agents, on kagent.

Before you start: What this lab is not

The goal here is the builder. Security is out of scope, on purpose, and I want to be upfront about what that means:

  • kagent runs in its default unsecure auth mode, so every request acts as the same user.
  • The chart’s bundled PostgreSQL uses its built-in password.
  • The UI and API are reachable only through kubectl port-forward on 127.0.0.1.

That is fine for a laptop. It is not fine for a shared cluster, and I will come back to why that gap matters.

You need Docker, kind, kubectl, helm, jq and Ollama (alternatively, you can use your API Key for Claude, OpenAI, or any other provider, but we wanted to make it as cheap as possible). There is nothing to clone: you create every file as you go. Start in an empty folder:

mkdir kagent-agent-builder && cd kagent-agent-builder
Step 1: Pick a local model that can actually do it

This is the part that surprised me. Writing a valid Kubernetes manifest through a tool call is harder than chatting, and small models show it. In my runs, qwen2.5:7b-instruct invented its own tool block format, and qwen2.5:14b-instruct sometimes answered politely without ever calling the apply tool. qwen3-coder:30b-a3b got it right on every run, so that is the model this post uses:

ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M   # about 18 GB on disk

The cluster reaches Ollama at host.docker.internal:11434, which works out of the box with Docker Desktop. On Linux you have to change that host in the values file below to an address the kind node can reach. I have not tested that path.

If you prefer a hosted model, kagent’s Helm chart also has provider blocks for OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI and Gemini. Then it is no longer free, of course.

Step 2: Install kagent with a tool server that can only write Agents

Create the cluster:

kind create cluster --name kagent-builder

kagent ships a tool server with Kubernetes tools, and by default the chart gives its ServiceAccount cluster-admin. A builder backed by cluster-admin is a bad idea even on a laptop, so the values file changes that. Create it:

providers:
  default: ollama
  ollama:
    provider: Ollama
    model: "qwen3-coder:30b-a3b-q4_K_M"
    config:
      host: host.docker.internal:11434
      options:
        num_ctx: "32768"
kagent-tools:
  tools:
    enabledTools:
      - k8s
  rbac:
    readOnly: true
    additionalRules:
      - apiGroups: ["kagent.dev"]
        resources: ["agents"]
        verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
grafana-mcp: {enabled: false}
k8s-agent: {enabled: false}
kgateway-agent: {enabled: false}
istio-agent: {enabled: false}
promql-agent: {enabled: false}
observability-agent: {enabled: false}
argo-rollouts-agent: {enabled: false}
helm-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-policy-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-manager-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-debug-agent: {enabled: false}

The model becomes the default ModelConfig. The tool server loads only its Kubernetes tools (22 of them). And it gets a read-only role plus one extra rule: it may write agents.kagent.dev, nothing else. The last block turns off the sample agents the chart installs by default, so the UI only shows yours.

Install the CRDs and kagent 0.10.2 with that file, and wait for the pods:

helm upgrade --install kagent-crds oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent-crds \
  --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \
  --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --create-namespace
helm upgrade --install kagent oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent \
  --kube-context kind-kagent-builder \
  --version 0.10.2 --namespace kagent --values kagent-values.yaml
for d in kagent-controller kagent-ui kagent-tools; do
  kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent rollout status deploy/$d --timeout=300s
done
Step 3: The builder is just an agent

This is the whole builder. Create the file:

apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: agent-builder
  namespace: kagent
spec:
  description: Builds new kagent agents from a plain-language description and deploys them.
  type: Declarative
  declarative:
    modelConfig: default-model-config
    stream: false
    systemMessage: |
      You build kagent agents. The user describes, in plain language, an agent
      they want. You turn that into ONE Kubernetes manifest and apply it. Do not
      ask follow-up questions: pick sensible defaults and go.
      How you work, in this order:
      1. List the existing agents with k8s_get_resources (resource_type
         agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent). Pick a name that is not taken;
         never overwrite an existing agent.
      2. Write the manifest in exactly the shape below and apply it with
         k8s_apply_manifest. The user confirms the apply in the UI; that is
         expected.
      3. Read it back with k8s_get_resource_yaml (resource_type
         agents.kagent.dev, namespace kagent) and look at the Accepted and
         Ready conditions in its status. Ready can take a few seconds.
      The manifest must be exactly this shape, and nothing else:
        apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
        kind: Agent
        metadata:
          name: 
          namespace: kagent
          labels:
            app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: agent-builder
        spec:
          description: |-
            
          type: Declarative
          declarative:
            modelConfig: default-model-config
            stream: false
            systemMessage: |
              
            tools:
              - type: McpServer
                mcpServer:
                  apiGroup: kagent.dev
                  kind: RemoteMCPServer
                  name: kagent-tool-server
                  toolNames: []
      Read-only tools you may give it: k8s_get_resources, k8s_get_resource_yaml,
      k8s_describe_resource, k8s_get_events, k8s_get_pod_logs.
      Never another kind, never another namespace, never write or delete tools,
      never more than one document.
      YAML that does not break: free text always goes in a block scalar, as in
      the shape above (description with |-, systemMessage with |). In a plain
      scalar, a colon followed by a space makes the YAML invalid, and a space
      followed by # silently cuts the value short.
      When something goes wrong:
      - If the user rejects the apply, do not retry it and do not read the
        agent back. Say it was not applied, and stop.
      - Never create a second resource with another name (-test, -check, -v2)
        to find out what failed. It tells you nothing and leaves clutter.
      - Do not name a cause you have not checked. An opaque error is not proof
        of a name clash, a permission problem or a network issue.
      - Report the error exactly as the tool returned it, and stop.
      When it is done, answer in three short lines: the agent's name, what it
      does, and which tools it can use. Then one more line with its real state
      from step 3 (Accepted, Ready). Never claim it is ready if it is not.
    tools:
      - type: McpServer
        mcpServer:
          apiGroup: kagent.dev
          kind: RemoteMCPServer
          name: kagent-tool-server
          toolNames:
            - k8s_apply_manifest
            - k8s_get_resources
            - k8s_get_resource_yaml
          requireApproval:
            - k8s_apply_manifest
    a2aConfig:
      skills:
        - id: build-agent
          name: Build an agent
          description: Turns a plain-language description into a deployed kagent agent.
          tags: [builder, agents]
          examples:
            - "Create an agent for the support team that answers questions about the state of the services in the cluster"

Apply it and wait until kagent reports it Ready:

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder apply -f agent-builder.yaml
kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent wait --for=condition=Ready \
  agent/agent-builder --timeout=300s

The tools block at the end is where the builder gets its limits. toolNames is an allowlist: of the 22 tools on the server, the model sees three. requireApproval is kagent’s human-in-the-loop switch. When the agent calls a tool on that list, the run pauses and the user has to approve or reject the call.

The system prompt does the rest. It tells the model to list existing agents first, so it never overwrites one, and then gives it the exact manifest shape it may produce: one Agent, in the kagent namespace, with a label that marks it as built by the builder, and only read-only tools. It also carries a few lessons I learned the hard way. Free text goes in YAML block scalars, because a colon followed by a space inside a plain string breaks the manifest. And when something fails, the model must report the error and stop, not create my-agent-v2 to see what happens.

Keep in mind that the prompt is a request, not a guarantee. The guarantees are the allowlist, the approval and RBAC.

Step 4: Ask for an agent

Open the UI:

kubectl --context=kind-kagent-builder -n kagent port-forward \
  --address 127.0.0.1 svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080

Go to http://localhost:8080, pick agent-builder and ask for something:

about the state of the services in the cluster

After half a minute or so the run stops. The UI shows the manifest the model wants to apply and two buttons.

Figure 2: The UI showing the manifest requiring user approval before applying.

  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"1","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Create an agent that lists the pods that are not running in the kagent namespace"}]}}}' \

jq -r '.result.status.state' build.json    # input-required

  -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":\"2\",\"method\":\"message/send\",\"params\":{\"message\":{\"role\":\"user\",\"messageId\":\"2\",\"taskId\":\"$TASK\",\"contextId\":\"$CTX\",\"parts\":[{\"kind\":\"data\",\"data\":{\"decision_type\":\"approve\"}}]}}}" \
  | jq -r '.result.status.state'            # completed

items.title: Phishing emails are baiting your AI assistant
items.summary: You ignored the suspicious email. You didn’t open the attachment, click the link, or reply to the sender. Then you asked your AI assistant to summarize your inbox. Could the message you wisely avoided find its way back onto your to-do list—only this time presented as an urgent recommendation from a tool you trust? That’s the risk behind phishing emails containing hidden instructions aimed at AI assistants. Instead of relying only on persuading you, attackers are also trying to influence the software that reads your messages. Recent research from Barracuda describes emails designed to target both audiences at once. For the human recipient, there was a password-protected attachment, with the password supplied in the email. For an AI assistant processing the message, there were hidden instructions intended to influence how it summarized or handled the content. By including a prompt injection , attackers give themselves another way to reach you. The malicious instructions could try to make the assistant describe the email as legitimate or urgent, encouraging you to revisit it. In another example, a hidden block instructed a summarizing AI to add a fake priority action: Change a vendor’s payment details. That could result in an employee sending money to an attacker’s account. The attacker isn’t simply asking the AI to repeat a fraudulent request. They’re trying to turn that request into the assistant’s recommendation. How prompt injection works Prompt injection means planting instructions in material an AI system is supposed to read, hoping it will follow those instructions instead of treating them as part of the material. When the instructions arrive through an outside source, such as an email or webpage, it’s often called indirect prompt injection. The malicious instructions don’t have to appear as ordinary, readable paragraphs. Barracuda identified concealment techniques including comments in the email’s underlying HTML code, text made invisible through styling, encoded content, and invisible “zero-width” characters. These can obscure instructions from a person viewing the message while leaving content available for an AI system to process. Whether that content actually reaches the model depends on how the particular tool extracts and prepares the email. That means this problem cannot be solved simply by asking people to look more carefully at their emails. Part of the defense must sit inside the tools handling those messages. Apollo Raines , developer of the AI code review service ShipItClean , explains: “The real flaw is that the model can’t tell the difference between text it’s supposed to read and instructions it’s supposed to follow. Stripping hidden content before it reaches the model is worth doing, and every vendor should do it. But it’s an arms race. Each new encoding trick is a new hole.” He adds: “People have learned to distrust the email. They haven’t learned to distrust their AI assistant. So, the defense has to live inside the tools. I’d go one step further: some of it has to live inside the model itself. Wrappers, filters, sandboxing and human sign-off on payments are all necessary.” Before taking action An assistant that summarizes messages could mislead you about which email deserves attention or what action it requires. An assistant with additional permissions could create a more serious problem. Depending on its capabilities and safeguards, malicious instructions might try to make it carry out unauthorized actions or disclose sensitive information . You don’t need to abandon AI tools that help with email. But you do need to consider what you trust them to do and what permissions you give them. The familiar phishing advice still applies. When an assistant reads your inbox on your behalf, check its recommendations before acting: Check the original message before acting on a recommendation involving money or sensitive information. If a summary tells you to pay an invoice, change account details, or share sensitive information, don’t treat the summary itself as verification. Always verify payment changes through a separate, established channel. Contact the person or organization using details you already trust, rather than relying on information supplied in the suspicious message. Keep your AI assistant’s permissions limited to what you need and, at work, what your organization allows. An assistant used to summarize emails should not need broad authority to carry out unrelated actions. Limiting access can reduce the consequences if it follows malicious instructions. Require human approval for high-impact actions like payments and changes to vendor payment details. Approval should include checking the underlying request, not simply accepting the assistant’s recommendation. From reporting threats to removing them. items.title: NVIDIA DCGM Exporter Bug Exposes GPU Servers to Resource Exhaustion Attacks
items.summary: NVIDIA patched high-severity flaw CVE-2026-47483 in DCGM Exporter that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to exhaust server resources, crash GPU monitoring , and disrupt AI workloads. DCGM Exporter is a common monitoring tool for GPU servers and Kubernetes clusters. It reads details such as GPU model, temperature, memory use, power draw, errors, and workload activity, then serves the data in a Prometheus-friendly format over HTTP. A unique UUID also lists each GPU. If this endpoint is public, an outsider can map valuable hardware, watch busy periods, and learn details about the software and workloads around it. The weakness sits in Go profiling routes under /debug/pprof. These routes were meant to help developers inspect CPU and memory use. However, vulnerable builds exposed them without login checks or safe request limits. By sending many profiling requests at once, an attacker could cause uncontrolled memory and CPU use until the exporter slowed, stopped responding, or crashed. NVIDIA DCGM Exporter Bug Exposes NVIDIA rated the issue 8.2 out of 10 and classified it as CWE-770 , which covers resource allocation without proper limits. A crash would remove the live view of GPU health, errors, temperature, and use. The same resource pressure could also slow nearby AI tasks when the exporter lacks strict container or host limits. The researchers tested the resource exhaustion only in a controlled environment and did not target the public systems they found. Shodan scans found 2,100 exposed DCGM Exporter hosts revealing 12,000+ GPU UUIDs over unauthenticated HTTP (source : lava.security ) Lava Security researcher Michael Katchinskiy found the flaw while studying public DCGM Exporter systems. Four internet scans between March and May 2026 identified about 2,100 hosts serving metrics without authentication. They exposed more than 12,000 unique GPU identifiers across about 300 organizations. Around one quarter of the DCGM hosts also exposed the risky profiling routes. The visible hardware included H100, H200, B200, Blackwell Ultra B300, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090 GPUs. The United States accounted for 5,274 exposed GPUs, or 44 percent of the observed total. Exposed AI infrastructure uses both NVIDIA H100/H200 accelerators and consumer RTX 4090/5090 GPUs (source : lava.security ) Researchers also found customer-run endpoints on networks linked to GPU cloud providers, including Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data, DigitalOcean, and others. The providers helped alert customers after receiving the findings. The case shows why AI monitoring ports should receive the same care as other management services. Cyber Security News has previously covered NVIDIA GPU driver flaws that enable code execution and published an AI data center security checklist covering GPU, firmware, and management-layer risks. NVIDIA’s security bulletin directs DCGM Exporter users to install version 4.8.2 or later. Operators should also keep –enable-pprof disabled unless profiling is needed. Exposed GPU exporters appeared on 2,000+ hosts across nearly 300 organizations (source : lava.security ) Exporter, Prometheus, and Node Exporter services should bind to a private or loopback interface and accept traffic only from approved monitoring systems through firewall rules, cloud security groups, or Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. Security teams should review internet-facing port 9400, block public access to /debug/pprof, and inspect logs for repeated or long-running profiling requests. Sudden memory growth, CPU spikes, Prometheus scrape failures, or gaps in GPU alerts may signal probing or exploitation. Teams should confirm that patched containers are deployed across every GPU node, not merely updated in a registry or configuration file. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. items.title: Admin Password “123456” Led to 8.8 Million Danish CPR Data Breach
items.summary: A weak administrator password is linked to a major Danish data breach that exposed information tied to about 8.8 million national identification numbers . At least three accounts at Pays, an IT company on the island of Funen, reportedly used “123456”, including an administrator account. The case shows how poor security at a company with trusted access can place a national database at risk. Pays had permission to search Denmark’s Central Person Register, known as CPR. An attacker allegedly used that access to collect personal records rather than breaking directly into the register’s underlying systems. Danish CPR Breach Unfolded According to Politiken’s investigation , the hacker shared stolen data with the newspaper and claimed the password “123456” helped unlock access to CPR numbers and addresses. Politiken reported 8,749,975 records, explaining why coverage describes the breach as either 8.7 million or roughly 8.8 million. The reported data covered about 5.5 million living people and 3.3 million deceased people. Those rounded figures should not be read as an exact total. The CPR register holds personal information about people living in Denmark or previously registered there. The Copenhagen Post reported that the attacker gained access through a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly built two programs to retrieve CPR information and save it outside the system. These details remain attributed to the hacker’s account, not a published forensic report. Access reportedly began on September 10 and lasted 21 days and 17 hours. That lengthy window raises questions about whether monitoring controls could detect repeated searches or unusual data collection before millions of records were exposed. Pays Confirms Misuse of Authorized Access Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 that its lawful access to search the CPR system had been abused. Managing director and owner Sophie Laursen acknowledged the attack in an email, according to The Copenhagen Post. Private companies and associations can receive CPR access when they have a legitimate need, such as checking customer or member addresses. This arrangement makes the security of each approved organization important, because valid credentials can provide a route into sensitive public records. The pattern resembles the Veradigm third-party data breach , where stolen vendor credentials allowed an attacker to download patient information through an approved interface. The systems differ, but both cases show why trusted access needs close limits and oversight. Cybersecurity News previously covered research into passwords used in RDP attacks , with “123456” leading the reported list. That research concerns remote desktop access, not Denmark’s CPR system, but highlights how predictable passwords remain useful to attackers. Organizations handling identity data should block common passwords, require unique credentials and enable multifactor authentication. Former employee accounts should be disabled promptly. Access should also be limited to necessary records, with alerts for unusual search volumes and bulk downloads. The breach also underlines the need to review partner access regularly, rather than treating approval as a permanent safeguard. The hacker told Politiken there were no plans to sell or publish the information. That claim does not remove the privacy risk created by unauthorized copies of personal records. The available reporting does not establish that exposed information has already been used for fraud, and it should not present such misuse as confirmed. Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. items.title: KFC Named in Gentlemen Ransomware Group’s Latest Breach Claim
items.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware group has allegedly claimed to have breached KFC, with a listing observed on October 10, 2026. The supplied alert identifies the target as United States KFC and places it in the hospitality sector. The claim remains unverified, and the available material does not establish a confirmed compromise of KFC’s U.S. systems. A public ransomware tracker also records KFC as being named by The Gentlemen on October 10. That supports the existence of the listing, rather than proving the reported intrusion. The supplied image shows KFC branding, the kfc.com domain, and a business description, but it contains no visible stolen files or technical evidence. The alert does not specify the amount of allegedly exposed data or the types of records involved. It also provides no entry method, ransom demand, affected systems, or evidence of file encryption. The October 10 observation date should therefore not be treated as the date attackers first entered a network. No KFC-specific malware hashes, attacker addresses, or verified attack timeline are provided. The image mainly describes KFC’s restaurant network, franchise model, sales, and suppliers. These business details do not demonstrate access to internal systems. The material does not identify whether the alleged target is a corporate network, a franchise operator, or another business connected to the brand. That scope remains an important unanswered question. The alert includes an ESIX score of 5.23, but supplies no explanation of its scoring method. The number cannot establish breach severity or confirm data theft. The supplied material and the sources reviewed for this report include no company confirmation, leaving the allegation pending independent verification. How The Gentlemen Operates Sophos tracks the operation behind The Gentlemen as GOLD SHERWOOD. Its researchers describe a ransomware service in which affiliates carry out attacks using the group’s tools. The operation uses double extortion, stealing data before encrypting files and then using the threat of publication to pressure victims into paying. In an analysis of 15 separate intrusions , Sophos found a repeated pattern involving rapid gains in access rights, legitimate remote access tools, data theft, and efforts to disable security controls. Some cases reached ransomware deployment within 24 hours of the first identified activity after compromise. These findings concern earlier cases, not the KFC allegation. Cyber Security News previously covered The Gentlemen’s efforts to disable endpoint detection and response tools and backup services . Attackers used vulnerable drivers and other utilities to stop security processes. They also changed Windows Defender settings and disrupted recovery tools, reducing the chance that defenders could detect the activity or restore encrypted systems. KFC’s parent company, Yum! Brands, previously disclosed a separate ransomware incident in January 2023. Cyber Security News reported that the attack disrupted systems, involved stolen information , and temporarily closed fewer than 300 restaurants in one market for one day. That historical incident does not confirm or explain the current claim. For security teams, Sophos recommends protecting remote access with multifactor authentication, patching exposed systems, watching changes to administrator accounts, and keeping backups protected. Investigators reviewing this allegation would need evidence tied to the affected organization, such as validated file samples, access logs, or a company statement.
